title: Last Stone Weight
problemStatement: You are given an array of integers stones representing stone weights. Repeatedly pick the two heaviest stones and smash them together: if they're equal, both are destroyed; otherwise the lighter is destroyed and the heavier becomes (heavy - light). Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.
approachSteps: You always need the CURRENT two largest stones, repeatedly — that 'always get the max, quickly, after updates' need is exactly what a max-heap provides.
Python's heapq is a min-heap, so negate all weights on insert (and negate back on read) to simulate a max-heap.
Push all stone weights (negated) into the heap.
While more than one stone remains: pop the two largest (heaviest), compute the result of smashing them, and if a stone remains (they weren't exactly equal), push it back.
When at most one stone remains, that's the answer (or 0 if the heap is empty).

bruteForce.approach: Sort the array on every iteration to find the two largest, remove them, and re-insert the result.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n^2 log n) — sorting repeated up to n times

optimalApproach: Max-heap (simulated via negation with Python's min-heap heapq): repeatedly pop the two largest, push back the difference if nonzero.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) — up to n-1 smashes, each involving O(log n) heap operations.
followUps: How would you adapt this if you needed to smash the two LIGHTEST stones instead (Last Stone Weight II is actually a different, DP-based problem — don't confuse the two)?
Why does negating values work to simulate a max-heap with Python's min-heap-only heapq?

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problemStatement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array (the kth largest in sorted order, not the kth distinct element).
approachSteps: Fully sorting the array to grab index -k is correct but does more work than necessary (O(n log n)) — you only actually need to know the top k elements, not the full order.
Maintain a MIN-heap of size k as you scan the array.

For each number, push it onto the heap; if the heap grows beyond size k, pop the smallest — this keeps exactly the k largest-seen elements in the heap at all times, with the smallest of THAT group sitting at the top.
After processing every number, the heap's smallest element (its top) is exactly the kth largest element overall.

bruteForce.approach: Sort the array descending and index k-1 (or ascending and index len-k).
bruteForce.spaceComplexity: O(1) to O(n) depending on sort

optimalApproach: Min-heap capped at size k; the heap's minimum after processing all elements is the kth largest. (An even faster average-case O(n) approach exists via Quickselect.)
timeComplexity: O(n log k) — n insertions/removals on a heap bounded to size k.
followUps: How would Quickselect (partition-based, like quicksort) solve this in average O(n) time — what's the trade-off versus the heap approach?
How would you handle this as a data STREAM, where numbers arrive one at a time and you need the kth largest after each?

title: Find Median from Data Stream
problemStatement: Design a data structure that supports adding integers from a stream and finding the median of all elements added so far, efficiently after each addition.
constraints: Up to 5*10^4 calls to addNum and findMedian
approachSteps: Sorting the whole stream on every findMedian call would be correct but wasteful (O(n log n) per call) — you want to maintain just enough structure to read the median in O(1).
Split all seen numbers into two halves: a max-heap holding the SMALLER half, and a min-heap holding the LARGER half — keep them balanced in size (differing by at most 1).
With that split, the median is always derivable from just the TOPS of the two heaps: if sizes are equal, average both tops; if unequal, the larger heap's top is the median.

On each addNum: push the new number into the max-heap (smaller half) first, then move its top into the min-heap (larger half) to maintain the ordering invariant (everything in the max-heap <= everything in the min-heap).
Then rebalance: if one heap has grown more than one element larger than the other, move its top element across to restore the size-balance invariant.

bruteForce.approach: Insert into a sorted list (or re-sort an array) on every addNum call, then read the middle directly.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n) per addNum with a sorted-insert list, or O(n log n) if re-sorting

optimalApproach: Two balanced heaps (a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half); the median is read directly from their tops in O(1), with O(log n) maintenance per insertion.
timeComplexity: O(log n) per addNum (heap push/pop); O(1) per findMedian.
spaceComplexity: O(n) total across both heaps to hold every number added.
followUps: Walk through why pushing into small first, then moving its top to large, keeps the max(small) <= min(large) invariant even when the new number belongs in the larger half.
How would you handle this if the data stream could also DELETE numbers, not just add them?
